752766.title: [UPDATED] Clean data beats more data (Open Pool v10 out now)
752766.author: Carrot Production
752766.content:
Update: full-size LB result on clean data, and Open Pool v10 is out

1. The leaderboard check I promised

I trained the same DeBERTa-v3-large recipe twice and changed only the training pool. Same hyperparameters, same epochs, same inference notebook.

Training pool Passages Public LB
Raw public pool (v7) 254k 0.585
Open Pool v9 (clean) 193k 0.587
  • 25% fewer passages, same or slightly better score. The 70k rows I removed were not helping the model.
  • +0.002 is within LB noise. Identical code can move by about 0.009 between submissions (thanks to alexchilton for measuring this). So the honest claim is: clean data matches the raw pool at three quarters of the size. At equal size, the controlled test in the post above showed +0.027.

2. Do not judge data changes with pool-based validation

My internal validation said v9 was clearly worse (0.629 → 0.591). The LB disagreed. I have seen this before: a model trained on a bigger, dirtier pool scored higher on validation but lower on the LB (0.611 vs 0.624).

dhruvtibarewal reported the same pattern in [753177]: OOF went from 0.569 to 0.605 and the LB went from 0.651 to 0.647. If your validation rewards data that looks like the pool, it will keep rewarding junk. For data decisions, the LB (or a test-shaped OOF, see GoPain's comment in [753177]) is the referee.

3. Open Pool v10: 198,507 clean passages

Open Pool v10 is v9 plus 5,581 new passages from 6 openly licensed datasets published since yesterday. They passed exactly the same filters, and every v9 row is unchanged.

Source New passages
abdullah1afify/ntl-generations (mostly the 5 Claude labels) 2,574
zitaoxu2002/ntl-proxy-passages-pre-ruling 1,026
carlosoponce/ntl-own-proxy-passages 973
aswathvanan/ntl-proxy-passages 474
elliotthankinson/ntl-exact-gens-v3 367
lucasboesen/ntl-free-proxy-generations 167
  • Most of it goes where it is needed: each Claude label gets about 500 to 1,000 more passages.
  • The same filters removed 1,396 candidate rows, mainly:
    • 885 em dashes on labels that never use them in train;
    • 239 passages too close to train content;
    • 181 passages cut off mid-sentence.
  • Not added:
    • a new OpenAI-response dataset whose licence for the generated text is not established yet;
    • one source with no documentation of how it was generated;
    • two re-merges of sources that were already in the pool or were removed in v9.
  • style_score for the new rows comes from the same style model, rebuilt exactly. New rows average 0.27, against 0.26 for v9.
  • Ids continue from ntlop_263484, so your v9 splits still work. To drop the new rows, keep ids below that.
import pandas as pd
pool = pd.read_parquet("/kaggle/input/name-that-llm-open-pool/ntl_open_pool.parquet")
print(len(pool))                      # 198,507: train on all of it
v9_only = pool[pool.id < "ntlop_263484"]

4. Still missing

glm-5.3, glm-5.3-flash, kimi-k3, qwen3.8-max and claude-fable-5 received almost nothing new. If you have openly licensed generations for these labels, please publish them and comment here. I will add them in the next version and credit you.

If this pool helps you, an upvote on the dataset helps others find it. And if you see something wrong in my method or numbers, please tell me. I would rather be corrected than wrong in public.

comments.author: GoPain
comments.content:
Thanks for the controlled comparison and for calling +0.002 noise. One thing that may help with reading such pairs: the noise of a difference between two submissions is not the noise of one score. Both are scored on the same public rows, so only the rows where exactly one of the two is right move the gap. If f is that share, the sd of the public gap is about sqrt(f / n_public), which for ~1,200 public rows is:

f (rows where exactly one is right) 1% 2% 5% 10% 20%
sd of the public gap 0.003 0.004 0.006 0.009 0.013

You can measure f on your OOF before submitting: compare the two models' correctness row by row.

  • Two separately trained models (different pools, or even the same code with another seed) can easily disagree in correctness on 10-20% of rows. That gives an sd of 0.009-0.013, the size of the ~0.009 that alexchilton measured, and +0.002 says nothing either way, as you wrote.
  • Two blends that differ in one small weight are a different story. My 0.621 and 0.623 blends disagree in correctness on only 1% of OOF rows, so their gap has an sd of about 0.003. There, 0.002 is still under one sd, but a 0.01 gap would be over three sd, i.e. real.

I checked the formula by simulation (balanced accuracy, 18 classes, random 30% public split; it matched within ±6% everywhere) and put it in a CPU notebook, with a helper that estimates f from your own OOF predictions: https://www.kaggle.com/code/locdunhat/is-a-0-002-lb-gain-real

Caveat: it assumes independent rows. Real errors cluster by prompt and topic, so treat these numbers as a floor.

753177.title: Retrained the Qwen2.5-14B member of nlm-v27 on the 120k pool: OOF 0.569 → 0.605, public LB 0.651 → 0.647. Why?
753177.author: Harshita Kumari
753177.content:
I tried what looked like the obvious next step after nlm-v27 (0.651). The result went the wrong way, and I'd like to understand why before spending more compute.

Background

In nlm-v27, three members (q14v5, q8v5, ll8v5) were retrained on the 120k nlm_pool_v5. That step took the notebook from 0.619 to 0.651.

The Qwen2.5-14B member (q25_14, Nishant's part-two checkpoint, weight 1.0) was not retrained. According to the author's member table, it was still trained on the old ~35k pool, with OOF 0.569.

What I did

I retrained only that member, with the same two-stage LoRA24 recipe as the other v5 members:

  • Model: Qwen2.5-14B base, first 32 of 48 layers, final norm off.
    • LoRA r16 / alpha 32 on q, k, v, o, gate, up and down.
    • Mean pool (first token masked) of layers 3, 5, 8, 11, 16, 21, 27 and 32, with a LayerNorm per layer.
    • A plain head and a prompt-centred head; batches are triplets of answers to the same prompt.
  • Stage 1: 1 epoch on all of nlm_pool_v5 (119,899 passages), class-weighted, lr 1e-4 (LoRA) / 1e-3 (heads), cosine.
  • Stage 2: 2 epochs on the official train, lr 5e-5 / 5e-4.
    • 5 prompt-grouped folds for OOF, plus a full-data fit for inference.
    • max_len 384, <|endoftext|> appended.
  • Hardware: about 2.3 h on one H100.

Results

Old q25_14 (Nishant, ~35k pool) Retrained (v5 pool)
Stage 1 only, on all official train — 0.570
5-fold OOF balanced accuracy 0.569 0.605 (folds 0.617 / 0.601 / 0.606 / 0.600 / 0.604)
In-sample check inside nlm-v27 — 0.95

Leaderboard: in nlm-v27 I changed one line, nmeta('lora_qwen25_14b') → my checkpoint, keeping weight 1.0 and everything else unchanged.

  • The log confirms it loaded correctly: l24 q25_14: adapter ... done (bf16 redo batches 0), in-sample acc 0.95.
  • Public LB: 0.647, against 0.651 for the original.

My guesses (happy to be corrected)

  1. Noise. The author reported identical notebooks scoring 0.600 and 0.605, and ATLAS is time-budgeted, so the scored rows can vary between reruns. A −0.4 change may be inside that.
  2. Lost diversity. The old member saw a different, smaller data mix, so its errors differed from q14v5, q8v5 and ll8v5. Trained on the same v5 pool, the new one may mostly repeat their errors. A stronger but more correlated member could add less than a weaker, independent one.
  3. Blend weights. The ensemble weights (plus Sinkhorn and ATLAS gating) were chosen with the old member in place.

Questions

  • Has anyone else seen a member improve clearly in OOF but not in the ensemble here? Is there a reliable way to judge "does this help the blend" offline, with only 2,699 rows?
  • Is there an estimate of the hidden-rerun noise for nlm-v27 (the same version submitted twice)?
  • Would keeping both models (old Nishant q25_14 at 1.0 plus the retrained one at a lower weight) be the better test of the diversity explanation?

Credits: dhruvtibarewal (nlm-v27, v5 pool and adapters), Nishant Dahal (two-stage recipe and part-two checkpoints), nuridudak (122k clean pool), and the LoRA24 recipe authors.

https://www.kaggle.com/code/harshitakumari256/nlm-v27?scriptVersionId=362705244

We measured something close to this with zero-weight ablations on the hidden test. Each run is the same notebook with one member's blend weight set to 0. Rescoring the same predictions gave the same score in our runs (two versions of an nlm-v21 fork both scored 0.617), so these deltas are not rerun noise.

On a part-two-based blend (0.638):

  • Removing the old Nishant q25_14, which has OOF 0.569 and only weight 0.2 there, cost -0.014 (plain head alone -0.010). That is about as much as the 0.611-OOF Qwen3-14B member's plain head (-0.017).
  • The n-gram SVC (OOF 0.473) cost -0.011.

So a weak but differently trained member carries far more LB weight than its OOF suggests.

On nlm-v27 without Llama (0.642), adding is not the mirror of removing:

  • Adding the author's ModernBERT-large (OOF 0.588) at weight 1.5 gave -0.004.
  • Our own Mistral-7B two-stage LoRA24 on the same v5 pool (OOF 0.578) at weight 1.0 gave +0.002.

Both fit your diversity and blend-weight guesses. Replacing the one member trained on a different data mix with a v5-pool clone removes exactly what the others don't already have. I'd try keeping the old q25_14 at 1.0 and adding yours at around 0.3-0.5. That is your third question, and I think it is the right test.

comments.author: GoPain
comments.content:
On your first question (judging "does this help the blend" offline with 2,699 rows): I tried scoring the OOF on a test-like shape rather than on all 18 answers per prompt, and I can share how that held up across 15 submissions, including a day when it did not.

Why it matters at all: if something in the blend depends on the other passages of the same prompt (the prompt-centred head in nlm-v27, ATLAS, Sinkhorn), the full-prompt OOF scores it on groups of 18, while the hidden test seems to have far fewer passages per prompt. So inside each validation fold I cut every prompt to m random answers, rebuild the groups the way the test side builds them (content clustering in my case), and score the whole pipeline; 15 draws per m.

All 15 submissions are one blend family: a LoRA member with a centred twin head (weight t), plus LoRA/DeBERTa/n-gram members, public LB 0.593–0.621. Correlation of each OOF version with the public LB (Pearson / Spearman):

OOF version first 10 submissions next 5 (chosen by m = 2) all 15
all answers (m = 18) 0.13 / −0.42 0.56 / 0.72 0.13 / −0.17
m = 6 0.44 / −0.26 0.64 / 0.87 0.45 / −0.09
m = 3 0.71 / 0.15 0.13 / 0.36 0.70 / 0.25
m = 2 0.91 / 0.82 −0.22 / 0.05 0.79 / 0.58
mean of the four 0.63 / −0.10 0.47 / 0.62 0.64 / 0.14

What I take from it:

  • After the first 10 I switched to ranking by m = 2, picked the next 5 with it, and it did not predict their order. Part of that is selection: I took the top of a 162-configuration grid by m = 2, so their m = 2 scores are inflated and squeezed together (0.6265–0.6328), and the LB spread of those 5 (0.611–0.621) is not far from LB noise.
  • Over all 15, m = 2 is still the version that agrees best, but much of that comes from one easy outlier (the twin member on its own, LB 0.593). Without it, Spearman drops to 0.49 for m = 2 and is around zero or negative for the rest. So it is a weak signal, useful mostly to reject clearly worse configurations, not to rank close ones.
  • The clearest pattern was about the centred head rather than the metric: the full-prompt OOF kept preferring a heavier head (t = 1.5–2.0), and all five of those lost on the LB to t = 1.0. Both submissions with t below 1.0 on the last day lost too. If you test the q25_14 swap or anything else prompt-dependent, I would check that its gain does not shrink when prompts are cut to 2–3 answers before trusting the full-prompt number.

Caveats: one blend family, 15 points, one public LB split; treat it as a sanity check, not a calibrated tool. For a blend with no prompt-dependent step, cutting prompts only subsamples rows and should not change the ranking.

754426.title: Harden a fork, then measure every part on the hidden test: my cheap ablation workflow
754426.author: HALX2158
754426.content:
Once my ensemble came from public forks, CV stopped telling me which parts mattered. This is the workflow I use now. All numbers are from my own runs.

1. Make submissions cheap

The scoring rerun did not use my weekly GPU quota; only the commit run did (175 s used, both before and after a roughly 2 h scoring run). The public test has only 3 rows, so on the commit run I write a placeholder and skip the model cells:

LIGHT = os.environ.get('KAGGLE_IS_COMPETITION_RERUN') is None and len(test) < 50

That cut my commit from about 1.8 h to 167 s. The rerun still runs everything: the full and light commits of the same pipeline both scored 0.617.

2. Guard against what a light commit can't catch

A light commit doesn't prove that the rerun will work. I lost submissions or GPU time to these:

  • Input paths: a Kaggle Model doesn't keep the dataset's top folder name, so an upstream glob can miss your mirror. I now run a free CPU script of about 1 minute that checks every lookup first.
  • Docker image: one upstream notebook pinned an image whose torch had no CUDA. The commit passed, then the reruns failed after 3 h. Add assert torch.cuda.device_count() > 0 to the light path.
  • Optional parts: give them a deadline, and treat a failure like a timeout by dropping the part. Never assert returncode == 0.
  • Slow loads: load_file on LoRA adapters read from a Dataset mount took about 100 s each, against 24 s in the author's log. Copying the adapters to /tmp took 34 s and cut my main pipeline from 4,884 s to 2,866 s (author: 2,859 s), with identical predictions.

I put these guards into a small CPU notebook you can copy from, with sample output for each: ntl-fork-guard-utility.

3. Measure parts by removing them

I set one part's blend weight to 0 and submit it with a light commit, about 3 minutes of GPU per variant. Two results on a 0.638 base:

Removed Public LB Delta
ATLAS (10% blend) 0.629 −0.009
Sinkhorn balancing 0.636 −0.002

Across the 10 variants I tried, every removal lowered the score, and weak but different models mattered more than their solo CV suggested.

Limits

  • It uses up submission slots, so I run 2–3 a day and keep a reserve.
  • It measures only the public part of the test, and scores are rounded to 3 decimals, so I don't read much into a delta of 0.001–0.002.
  • Parts can substitute for each other: two similar parts can each look small alone and large when removed together, so test groups too.
  • Removing is not the mirror of adding. See my next post.

752365.title: Sinkhorn balancing: what it costs when the test mix is uneven
752365.author: Boris Konstantinovskii
752365.content:
Many public notebooks end with Sinkhorn balancing: the test probabilities are rescaled until every class gets the same total mass. For balanced accuracy this is a sensible correction if the test is close to even. We do not know the hidden test's mix, so we measured what balancing costs when the mix is uneven.

Setup.

  • Out-of-fold probabilities of a strong blend: 2,699 passages, prompt-grouped 5-fold CV, about 0.64 balanced accuracy.
  • Test pools of 2,000 passages, the model mix drawn from a symmetric Dirichlet(alpha), 40 pools per setting. Alpha 1 is a very uneven mix, with some models nearly absent. Alpha 100 is nearly even.
  • On each pool: the plain argmax, and Sinkhorn at 1, 3 and 50 iterations.
test mix plain 1 iteration 3 iterations 50 iterations
exactly even (all OOF rows) 0.6387 0.6398 0.6409 0.6379
alpha 100, nearly even 0.6384 0.6391 0.6395 0.6363
alpha 20 0.6357 0.6376 0.6379 0.6298
alpha 5 0.6393 0.6391 0.6384 0.6167
alpha 1, very uneven 0.6361 0.6345 0.6284 0.5704

Small pools are worse still. On a sparse CV scheme (about 75 passages per pool, 1 to 4 per prompt, uneven mix), full balancing took the same blend from 0.645 to 0.475.

What we take from it.

  • Full balancing is a bet that the test is close to even. If it is, you gain a few thousandths. If it is not, you can lose several points.
  • A partial balance is a cheap hedge. One to three iterations keep most of the gain on an even test and lose under 0.01 on the most uneven mix we tried.
  • OOF predictions cannot show the gain some people see on the LB. OOF rows carry no shift between train and test, so this measures the risk only. If balancing helps you on the public LB, that says your test predictions lean towards some models. It says nothing about the test's mix.

To check your own blend, take its OOF log-probabilities and labels:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

def sinkhorn(logp, iters):
    """Rescale log-probabilities until every class gets the same total mass; rows stay normalised."""
    z, target = logp.copy(), np.log(len(logp) / logp.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        m = z.max(0, keepdims=True)
        z = z - (m + np.log(np.exp(z - m).sum(0, keepdims=True))) + target
        z = z - z.max(1, keepdims=True)
        z -= np.log(np.exp(z).sum(1, keepdims=True))
    return z

def uneven_pools(y, alpha, size=2000, draws=40, seed=0):
    """Row indices of test pools whose class mix is drawn from a symmetric Dirichlet(alpha)."""
    rng, classes = np.random.default_rng(seed), np.unique(y)
    by_class = [np.flatnonzero(y == c) for c in classes]
    for _ in range(draws):
        counts = rng.multinomial(size, rng.dirichlet([alpha] * len(classes)))
        yield np.concatenate([rng.choice(ix, k) for ix, k in zip(by_class, counts) if k])

# logp: (n, 18) OOF log-probabilities, y: (n,) labels, labels: class names in column order
for alpha in [1, 5, 20, 100]:
    scores = np.mean([[balanced_accuracy_score(y[r], labels[sinkhorn(logp[r], k).argmax(1)]) for k in (0, 1, 3, 50)]
                      for r in uneven_pools(y, alpha)], axis=0)
    print(alpha, scores.round(4))

comments.author: HALX2158
comments.content: One LB data point to set against your CV table: on a 0.638 blend, turning off the final Sinkhorn (300 iterations, so full balancing) and changing nothing else gave 0.636 on the public LB. So full balancing was worth +0.002 there, on the public part only. That is in line with your "few thousandths" on an even test, though as you say it shows how our test predictions lean, not what the test's mix is. I haven't tried 1 to 3 iterations on the LB.

comments.author: GoPain
comments.content:
Thanks, this matches what I see. One addition: what Sinkhorn removes is a per-class offset in the scores, so the same gain can be learned on OOF and applied to test without any assumption about the test mix.

Cross-fitted offsets: learn one log-offset per class on four folds' OOF (Sinkhorn on those rows, keep the column scalings), add them to the fifth fold's scores, then argmax. My grouped 5-fold OOF (2,699 rows):

argmax Sinkhorn, all rows cross-fitted offsets
DeBERTa-v3-large, two-stage 0.521 0.564 0.560
Qwen3-8B LoRA 0.595 0.600 0.599
LoRA + 0.5 DeBERTa + 1.0 n-gram SVC 0.626 0.626 0.621
  • A single member with strong class preferences (the DeBERTa here) gets almost all of its Sinkhorn gain from offsets learned on OOF. Offsets learned that way do not care what the test mix is.
  • On a blend whose members lean in different directions, little is left to remove: plain argmax already equals Sinkhorn on OOF. Cross-fitted offsets only add noise (−0.005). Full balancing then buys nothing on CV and keeps the risk you measured.
  • On the public LB, Sinkhorn on an earlier LoRA alone gave +0.011 (0.538 to 0.549) while its OOF did not move (0.5760 to 0.5761). That fits your last point: the LB gain reflects how test predictions lean, not the test's mix.

I checked the same comparison on a known-truth simulation (18 Gaussian classes with per-class offsets). On a balanced test, offsets from validation are within 0.003 of Sinkhorn. With a Dirichlet(1) test mix, Sinkhorn's regret against the Bayes rule rises to 0.060 while the offsets stay at 0.018. Estimating the test prior by EM and balancing towards it was worse than both. That is expected, because for balanced accuracy the optimal decision does not depend on the test prior. Notebook with the code and tables: https://www.kaggle.com/code/locdunhat/sinkhorn-rebalancing-under-balanced-accuracy

754131.title: My popular ATLAS adapter vs Uniform Smoothing
754131.author: Joseph Adamski
754131.content:
My ATLAS adapter dataset has been downloaded 4,636 times (ATLAS is the method developed by Ko et al.; these are my independently trained weights). You can find my public notebook here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/josephadamski91/teach-the-model-10-atlas

Does ATLAS help because it recognizes which model wrote a passage, or because it makes the combined predictions less overconfident?

I tested this by replacing ATLAS’s predictions with an equal guess across all 18 models. I kept the same blend weight and the steps that turn those probabilities into final answers.

Public leaderboard results

Notebook Blend weight Real ATLAS Equal-guess replacement ATLAS advantage
V31 / Omer’s scored v1 20% 0.663 0.662 +0.001
Teach the Model 10% 0.607 0.605 +0.002

Local tests

These scores come from passages with known answers, tested locally. They are not Kaggle leaderboard scores. Accuracy is averaged equally across the 18 models. All blends below use 10%.

Notebook / test set Without either blend Real ATLAS Equal-guess replacement How often both blends picked the same model
Full Hungarian — 640 passages 35.21% 33.54% 33.53% 638 / 640
Prompt v1 — 640 passages 28.50% 27.30% 27.42% 639 / 640
Lucas v3 — 640 passages 45.64% 45.49% 45.33% 639 / 640
Larger test — 2,210 passages / 539 prompts 33.57% 32.34% 32.25% 2,202 / 2,210

The equal-guess replacement produced almost exactly the same final answers as ATLAS locally. However, neither blend improved accuracy over using neither blend on these test sets. On Kaggle, real ATLAS scored slightly higher than the equal-guess replacement.

Separate runs may process different numbers of passages with ATLAS, and the older comparison required a restored checkpoint.

These results help explain what ATLAS might be doing, but they do not establish exactly how much of the benefit comes from recognizing the author versus reducing overconfidence.

TL;DR: Replacing ATLAS with an equal guess came surprisingly close to its score. That makes me think reducing overconfidence is part of the story, though these tests don’t settle it.

I entered this competition mainly to test on a specific use case and am now focused on another competition, but I wanted to share the results in case someone sticking around wants to investigate further.

754084.title: Ten LB points can't tell you which OOF to trust: a small simulation
754084.author: GoPain
754084.content:
Many of us score several offline versions of the same blend (full-prompt OOF, prompts cut to a few answers, a holdout) and check which one moves with the public LB. I did that and it went wrong for me: over ten submissions, one cut of my OOF had Spearman 0.82 with the LB. I picked the next five by it, and on those five its Spearman was 0.05 (details in a reply on 753177).

So I simulated the situation with a known ground truth. Each configuration has a latent quality. Each proxy tracks it with correlation rho, and the proxies can share part of their error, as cuts of one OOF matrix do. The LB tracks it with correlation r. Phase 1 submits n configurations and picks the proxy with the best Spearman; phase 2 submits the top 5 by that proxy. Notebook (CPU, under a minute): https://www.kaggle.com/code/locdunhat/which-offline-score-tracks-the-lb

What came out, for r = 0.7 and 10 phase-1 submissions:

  • The best-correlated proxy is often not the best proxy. When the proxies are close in quality, it is truly the best 28–41% of the time (chance is 25%). Well-separated proxies only reach 43–64%.
  • The winning correlation is inflated. On average it is 0.65, against a true 0.47. Four identical proxies show exactly the same inflation, so a high winning correlation tells you little.
  • A collapse on the next five is expected. On the five configurations a proxy ranks highest, its correlation with the LB averaged between −0.02 and 0.27 everywhere in the grid, even when it was truly the best proxy. Those five are about equally good, so LB noise sets their order. A proxy that "stopped working" may be as good as before.
  • Average or select, depending on shared error. If the proxies' errors are independent, averaging them beats even the best single one. If they share most of their error (cuts of the same OOF), averaging dilutes the best one. Then choosing by correlation pays off only once you have about 20 points.

What I do now: I only submit a change if it improves every cut of the OOF, not just the one that looked best on the LB, and I do not read much into the order of my top few submissions. The model is simple (Gaussian, no directional bias in the proxies, and LB noise independent across submissions, while a real public split is fixed), so treat the numbers as orders of magnitude.

Code and the 180,000 simulated seasons are public (CC0): https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/locdunhat/proxy-selection-simulations

754026.title: [ Ablation Note ] Why Prompt-Clustered Adaptive Centering + Target-Shrunk Sinkhorn-Knopp (ρ = 0.35) Outperform Uniform Marginal Forcing
754026.author: Pablo Diego Pereira
754026.content:
When scoring attribution models on GroupKFold(n_splits=5, groups=prompt_id) across all 2,699 training passages (18 models x 180 prompts), two distinct sources of error dominate:

  1. Shared Prompt Effect ($p_g$): Even strong classifiers shift their logit profiles according to topic domain and prompt-induced response length ($x_{gi} = \mu_c + p_g + \varepsilon_{gi}$).
  2. Marginal Collapse vs. Non-Uniform Test Priors: Uncalibrated linear and neural heads over-predict high-entropy generalist models, while naive uniform Sinkhorn-Knopp (target = 1/18) hurts on the leaderboard because Public/Private test class counts are unequal.

In our updated public notebook (Name That LLM Starter Notebook), we benchmarked each transductive layer step by step on 5-fold GroupKFold(prompt_id) before integrating them with the multi-backbone LoRA24 + Shared-Prompt Gaussian + ATLAS 20% ensemble:

Step Specification (5-Fold GroupKFold on prompt_id) OOF Balanced Accuracy Fold Std
1 Word TF-IDF (1..3-grams) baseline 0.3145 0.0153
2 + Character TF-IDF (char + char_wb) + 20 Stylometric Ratios 0.3367 0.0166
3 + LinearSVC + Stamatatos Topic Distortion (masking words outside top-100 function words) 0.3686 0.0155
4 + Prompt-Clustered Adaptive Centering (sim_thr=0.15, α=0.65$) 0.3812 0.0173
5 + Target-Shrunk Damped Sinkhorn-Knopp (α=0.45, ρ=0.35, 100 rounds) 0.3834 0.0136
6 + Within-Cluster Hungarian Assignment (linear_sum_assignment) 0.4345 0.0216

Key Takeaways:

  • Stamatatos Topic Masking (+0.0319 OOF): Replacing all vocabulary outside the top-100 English function words with * while keeping case and punctuation forces the secondary linear head to learn purely syntactic cadence rather than prompt nouns.
  • Target-Shrunk Sinkhorn-Knopp (τ=(1−ρ) π'_pred + ρπ _train with ρ=0.35 ρ=0.35): Shrinking predicted marginals partially toward empirical training priors rather than forcing uniformity improves both mean OOF accuracy and cuts fold-to-fold standard deviation by 21% (0.0173 -> 0.0136).
  • Family-Mass-Preserving Sibling Residual (V40A + V31): Applying 5-fold GroupKFold reliability-weighted stylometric tie-breaking strictly inside each provider family (claude, gemini, gpt, glm) via logsumexp conservation resolves sibling ties without perturbing cross-provider probabilities.

753779.title: [BIG UPDATE - please try it] Same data, +0.027 accuracy: 1 in 4 passages in the public NTL pool was junk or the wrong genre. I cleaned it (Open Pool v9)
753779.author: Carrot Production
753779.content:
TL;DR

  • I audited every passage in the public pool that most of us train on: 254k passages from 59 community datasets. About 1 in 4 passages a model learns from is junk or the wrong genre.
  • I trained the same small LoRA model on 45,000 passages each time and changed only which passages it saw. Cleaned data scored +0.026 to +0.027 balanced accuracy on real train passages. Both seeds agree.
  • The dirtier a label's data was, the more cleaning helped (Spearman 0.64). kimi-k3 gained +16 points of recall and claude-opus-4-8 +13.
  • Open Pool v9 is that clean set: 192,926 passages, 18 labels, ready to train. No filtering needed. The 70,558 removed rows are listed by id and reason in removed_rows.csv.

Please support this work and share your thinking. This research cost me a lot of GPU time and effort, all to build the best training data I can for the community. If I got anything wrong, please point it out and tell me your view.

1. What is wrong with the raw pool

I compared the pool with the competition's train.csv. This is the only data known to come from the host's own generation process. Each label is weighted equally.

In the raw pool (v7) Passages
Raw API responses (HTTP headers, JSON, x-generation-id) stored as text 13,114
Refusals ("I can't…", "As an AI…") 6,939
Cut off mid-sentence 15,963
Chat preambles ("Sure, here's…"), CJK text, length outside 36–275 words, same text with two labels 3,545
Off-genre sources: chat logs, benchmark answers, reasoning traces 46,672

Two of these deserve a closer look:

  • API dumps fill the model's context window with headers. 85% of the text you can pull out of these dumps is already in the pool as clean rows. You lose nothing by dropping them.
  • Off-genre text looks clean, but it teaches the wrong voice. A label's chat replies are not the same as that label's single-paragraph essays. In a balanced 45k sample of the raw pool, 27.7% of passages came from these sources. For some Claude labels it was more than half.

Real train passages never contain these. In train, 99.9% of passages end with punctuation; in the raw pool, 93% do. After cleaning the figure is 99.4%.

2. The test: same size, different quality

I wanted to measure quality only, so every run had the same setup:

  • Model: Qwen3-1.7B-Base with a LoRA classifier, trained for 1 epoch on the pool only.
  • Data: exactly 2,500 passages per label (45,000 total) in every run.
  • Score: balanced accuracy on all 2,699 train passages. The model never trains on them, so every prompt is unseen.
  • Repeats: 2 seeds per variant. Runs are deterministic: the same variant and seed reproduce to the 4th decimal.

Training data (45k passages each) Balanced acc. vs raw
Raw pool v1-5 0.466 —
Raw pool v1-7 0.464 −0.001
v1-5 minus hard junk (dumps, refusals, preambles) 0.474 +0.009
v1-5 minus junk and off-genre sources 0.493 +0.027
v1-7 minus junk and off-genre sources 0.492 +0.026

What this shows:

  1. Hard junk hurts. Removing it adds about +0.009.
  2. Off-genre text hurts more than obvious junk. Removing it adds another +0.019, even though those passages look clean.
  3. Newer pool batches are not the problem; their junk is. The raw v1-7 pool scores the same as raw v1-5, and the clean v1-7 pool scores the same as clean v1-5. If you saw a lower LB after adding newer rows, check what came with them.

3. It is the dirty labels that improve

Each dot is one label. The x-axis shows how much of that label's raw sample was junk or off-genre. The y-axis shows how much its recall changed after cleaning. Spearman correlation is 0.64:

  • kimi-k3: 46% contaminated, +16 recall
  • claude-opus-4-8: 51% contaminated, +13 recall
  • Labels that were already clean (most Gemini labels): little change

This is what you would expect if the junk itself was the problem.

4. Things we tried that did not help

These results are useful too, because they show what not to spend time on.

  • Keeping only the most "train-like" passages. I built a style-only scorer that tells train passages from pool passages using punctuation, pronouns, sentence rhythm and function words, never topic words. It reaches AUC 0.77–0.79 on prompts it never saw. I then dropped the 30% of each label's passages that looked least like train. The result was no gain (−0.004 balanced accuracy over 2 seeds, and −0.016 recall on the 8 hardest labels): the variety you lose costs more than the cleaner style earns. v9 includes the score as a column, so you can try other cut-offs yourself.
  • Dropping every passage generated through the Kaggle Benchmarks proxy. The host has ruled that the proxy may not be used to build training sets ([752084]). Removing about 70k such rows changed the score by −0.001 on average over 2 seeds, which is within noise. v9 flags them in flag_kb_proxy so you can stay on the safe side at almost no cost.
  • Cheap proxies for data quality are misleading. A TF-IDF + linear model trained on the same subsets said cleaning hurts. It rewards volume and does not care about genre. Only test data decisions with the kind of model you actually train.

5. What is still open: the prompt gap

One style gap does not move with cleaning. 31% of train passages use "we / our / us", against 15% in the pool, before and after cleaning. The cause is the host's prompts, not junk. Their prompts lead to a collective, explanatory voice more often than the prompt banks most of us used. If you generate new data, prompts closer to that voice are probably the next big win. Please share what you find.

6. How to use v9

import pandas as pd
pool = pd.read_parquet("/kaggle/input/name-that-llm-open-pool/ntl_open_pool.parquet")
print(len(pool), pool.model.value_counts())       # 192,926 clean passages, 18 labels: train on all of it
  • Every row is clean. v9 removes API dumps, refusals, preambles, off-genre sources, cut-off passages, rows with a licence or provenance problem, answers to train prompts, and typography a label never uses in train.
  • Row ids are unchanged from earlier versions, so your existing splits keep working. Removed ids and the reason for each are in removed_rows.csv, and the totals per reason are in removal_summary.csv.
  • Licences are clean too. Every row comes from a CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA 4.0 or CC0 dataset with verifiable provenance. About 38.8k rows that came from a licence-excluded source through CC0 re-uploads are gone.
  • flag_kb_proxy marks rows generated through the Kaggle Benchmarks proxy. They are kept because public community datasets are allowed; drop them in one line if you want to be strict (section 4).
  • style_score is the train-likeness score from section 4.
  • The numbers in this post ship with the dataset: dataq_results.csv, style_gap.csv, removal_summary.csv and the figures.

Caveats

  • These tests use a 1.7B model at a fixed 45k passages. Bigger models are more robust to noise, so the gain may be smaller at 14B scale. I am now training a full-size model on v9 and will report its LB score in this thread.
  • The clean set has about 20% fewer passages than the raw pool. At equal size clean wins clearly; at full size I am still measuring.
  • Balanced accuracy on train passages is not the LB. It is the closest held-out data we have, and every prompt in it is unseen during training.

Credit goes to everyone who published generations. This pool exists because of you. Questions, corrections and new open-licensed data for glm, kimi, qwen and claude-fable are all welcome.

753526.title: Stratified CV gives 0.13, prompt-grouped CV gives 0.31 (LB 0.308) for the same baseline
753526.author: Harshit Kumar
753526.content:
Same model (word 1-2 + char 1-5 TF-IDF, LinearSVC, class_weight balanced), two validation schemes, one fold seed:

  • prompt-grouped 5-fold: balanced accuracy 0.3126
  • plain stratified 5-fold: 0.1315
  • public LB of the same model trained on all of train: 0.308

Reproducible on Kaggle CPU in about 3 minutes: https://www.kaggle.com/code/harshitsama/name-that-llm-grouped-cv-beats-stratified-cv

Data facts from the notebook: 2,699 train rows, 18 models, 150 prompts, 149-150 rows per model, so every prompt is answered by (almost) every model. My explanation (not isolated with a separate experiment): a random split puts the other models' answers to the same prompt in training, which teaches prompt-topic words that point at the wrong label for the held-out answer. Grouping by prompt_id removes that and matches the test (unseen prompts).

If you tune on stratified folds you will be misled; group by prompt_id and average a few seeds of the group assignment (seed noise was about 0.001-0.004 in my runs). Corrections welcome.

750664.title: What the punctuation already tells you about the 18 models (and what it can't)
750664.author: Masood Ahmed
750664.content:
I spent my first day on a data audit instead of training anything, and honestly the punctuation table explains most of what makes this competition hard. Posting the numbers in case they save someone a day.

A few things I noticed:

Lab is almost readable from two columns. Claude and GLM love em dashes and only ever use straight quotes. GPT and Gemini are the opposite: curly apostrophes everywhere, straight quotes basically never. Gemini barely uses em dashes at all.

GLM looks like Claude on every single marker here. Which is probably why glm-5.3 and glm-5.3-flash are two of my three worst classes right now (recall 0.17 and 0.19). Punctuation can't separate them from Claude, so that has to come from word choice.

Siblings are flat. Inside OpenAI the em dash rate goes from 9% (gpt-6-astra) to 37% (gpt-5.6-luna), which is something, but not much. Inside Gemini the four models mostly differ on how often they use a curly apostrophe (6% to 31%). Everything else about the sibling problem lives somewhere other than punctuation.

On the error split: a plain TF-IDF (char 1-5 + word 1-2, lowercase=False) with logistic regression, validated with StratifiedGroupKFold on prompt_id, gets 0.345 balanced accuracy (CI 0.33 to 0.36, bootstrapped over prompts). If you only ask "did it get the lab right", the same predictions score 0.58, and 55% of all mistakes are the right lab, wrong model. I then added a char_wb affix view and about 80 hand-made typography and rhythm features (dash/quote variants, sentence length stats, type-token ratio) in a LightGBM and blended the three. That gets to 0.372 (CI 0.36 to 0.39), lab accuracy 0.61… and the within-lab share of errors actually goes UP to 58%. So the classical stuff is solving the easy lab problem and barely scratching the sibling problem.

Length matters more than I expected. Under 60 words the blend is at 0.27, over 160 words it's at 0.46. If your CV looks healthy, it's worth checking it by length bucket before trusting it.

Two things that did not work, since those are useful too. First-word habits aren't a tell here: every lab opens with "the" or "in" most of the time, so openers don't carry the signal some papers report. And the punctuation "rules" that look absolute in train (Gemini never using em dashes, Claude never using curly quotes) are exactly the kind of thing that breaks on freshly generated text, so I'm treating them as features to learn alongside everything else, not as hard filters.

For what it's worth, the top LightGBM features were comma rate, type-token ratio, word-length std, sentence-length std, capitalised-word rate and long-word rate. Vocabulary richness and rhythm, not any one mark.

All of this is grouped CV on the public train set only, 5 folds x 3 seeds, no external data. Happy to be corrected on any of it.

753053.title: Why grouped CV over-picks test-time centring, and a way to validate it against the test batch
753053.author: GoPain
753053.content:
Follow-up to my centring post (752708). There, the centring weight my prompt-grouped CV liked best (all members at 0.5, OOF 0.646) was the worst of four on the public LB (0.590 against 0.603 for weight 0.25), and the LB order followed my CV recomputed with prompts cut to two or three answers. I think I understand why now, and it applies to every test-time rule that clusters the test: centring, twin heads, Gaussian group heads.

Two things decide how well a cluster-centred rule works: how many passages a real prompt has in the batch, and how crowded the batch is. A validation fold here holds about 30 prompts. The hidden test, if it has the same structure, holds a few hundred. With content clustering at a fixed cut, a crowded batch merges more clusters across prompts, so the clusters are less pure than anything you see inside a fold, even with the same number of answers per prompt. A fold-level CV therefore sees cleaner clusters than the test has and picks heavier centring than the test wants.

I checked this on a known-truth simulation (style features with a shared group shift, groups found by clustering a separate content view, 33 settings of score centring and a centred twin head, regret against the best setting for each test batch, 20 worlds). Worst regret over six test batches (groups of 18, 6, 3 or 2 items, a mix of 1 to 18, mostly singletons):

how the setting is chosen worst regret
full groups (what grouped CV does) 0.037
groups cut to 2 and 3 0.061
mean over cuts 18 / 6 / 3 / 2 0.030
cuts matched to the test's cluster-size histogram 0.037
validation items clustered together with the unlabelled test 0.014

Matching the test's cluster sizes does not work by itself, because in a crowded batch of small prompts the merged clusters look large. What worked in every case was to put the validation passages into the unlabelled test batch, cluster everything together, and score only the validation passages. They then meet the same crowding and the same merges as the test. The prompt cut m can be chosen by matching the cluster-size histogram of the validation passages to the test passages'.

In this competition that is possible inside the inference notebook: the test texts are there, and saved OOF log-probabilities (or OOF features, for a twin head) of the train passages can be attached as a dataset. One can mix the train passages into the test, cluster, and pick the centring weight on the train passages before predicting. I have not run that yet.

Today's LB check, with a centred twin head (a second head trained on features minus their prompt mean, applied to features centred inside test content clusters) on my LoRA member, blended with the same three members as before:

blend OOF full / cut 3 / cut 2 public LB
yesterday's best (score centring w 0.25, no twin) 0.644 / 0.624 / 0.640 0.603
twin w 1.0 + other members 0.668 / 0.626 / 0.646 0.620
twin w 1.0, other members also score-centred 0.670 / 0.625 / 0.646 0.619
twin w 0.5, other members also score-centred 0.653 / 0.626 / 0.646 0.618
twin w 0.5, one member dropped 0.655 / 0.624 / 0.648 0.614
twin member alone 0.658 / 0.605 / 0.562 0.593

The LB order again follows the cut-3 column, but the LB gain over yesterday (+0.017) is far larger than the gain on the cut-2/3 columns (+0.002 / +0.007) and closer to the full-prompt one (+0.024). So the small cuts rank well but under-rate the twin, which fits the simulation: neither full groups nor small cuts alone is the right proxy. Until I have the embedded check running, I rank settings by the mean over cuts.

Code, tables and the dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/code/locdunhat/validating-test-time-centring-for-the-test-batch

Caveat: the simulation has a purely additive group shift and content independent of the author, so the regret sizes are not this competition's. The direction (fold CV over-picks centring) agrees with my LB result above.

comments.author: HALX2158
comments.content:
One more LB data point for twins. In a part-two-based blend (0.638) with two LoRA members, each with a centred twin:

  • Removing both twins cost -0.017. That is the same size as your +0.017 gain.
  • Removing either twin alone cost only about -0.003 to -0.004.

So the twins largely substitute for each other. Once one centred view is in the blend, a second one adds little on the LB, even if CV says otherwise.
